intro: The Fifth’s scherzo begins in the cellos and double basses, almost under its breath, then answers with a horn call. Its strangest stroke comes at the return: the horns’ challenge has become a whisper, and the timpani begin the long wait for the finale.

sections.label: A · Low strings and horn calls
sections.mNote: Low C-minor arpeggios, then repeated-note horn calls

sections.label: B · The basses start a fugue
sections.mNote: Running quavers climb through the strings in C major

sections.label: A′ · Plucked strings and quiet winds
sections.mNote: The horn rhythm returns in clarinets, bassoons and plucked strings

sections.label: Link · Timpani beneath held strings
sections.mNote: Repeated C leads into the finale without a break

cues.title: Cellos in the dark
cues.text: Cellos and double basses climb through the notes of C minor. A quiet answer comes from above, then a pause. The low strings try again. Beethoven leaves the three-beat dance suspended between these phrases.
cues.evidence: Beethoven, Symphony No. 5, Breitkopf & Härtel full score, plate B.5, printed p. 37: low-string arpeggios, orchestral replies and fermatas. https://s9.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/0/0c/IMSLP52624-PMLP01586-Beethoven_Werke_Breitkopf_Serie_1_No_5_Op_67.pdf
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: The horns remember
cues.text: Three short notes, then a long one: the horns bring back the rhythm that opened the symphony. Their repeated notes hammer at one pitch after the cellos’ climb through a chord.
cues.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel full score, printed pp. 37–38. The rhythmic connection is discussed by Eastman School of Music: https://www.esm.rochester.edu/beethoven/symphony-no-5/
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: The basses take off
cues.text: C major, and a running tune for cellos and double basses. The other strings take it up in turn, each new entry catching the previous one before it has finished. The players at the bottom of the orchestra have set everyone running.
cues.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel full score, printed pp. 42–46: C-major trio and imitative string entries.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: An enormous December concert
cues.text: Vienna, 22 December 1808: Beethoven introduces the Fifth and Sixth symphonies in the same concert at the Theater an der Wien. He also plays his Fourth Piano Concerto. The evening includes music from the Mass in C and ends with the Choral Fantasy.
cues.evidence: Eastman School of Music, Symphony No. 5, première details and concert programme: https://www.esm.rochester.edu/beethoven/symphony-no-5/

cues.title: The scherzo whispers
cues.text: The opening returns in C minor, with its voice lowered. Clarinets and bassoons exchange the repeated-note rhythm with plucked strings. The horn call has become something furtive, stepping through the same dance on tiptoe.
cues.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel full score, printed pp. 46–49: rewritten scherzo return, pianissimo winds and pizzicato strings.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Three trombones waiting
cues.text: Three trombonists, a piccolo player and a contrabassoon player wait through this movement. Beethoven saves their first notes for the finale. The orchestra still has another sound in reserve.
cues.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel full score: piccolo, contrabassoon and three trombones first appear in movement IV. Instrumentation also listed at https://www.esm.rochester.edu/beethoven/symphony-no-5/
cues.how: About the passage as a whole.

cues.title: C against A♭
cues.text: The timpani repeat C. Cellos and basses hold A♭ beneath the upper strings’ C, a strange place to wait for C major. The violins begin to stir; a long crescendo carries the music straight into the finale.
cues.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel full score, printed pp. 50–52: A♭ in the low strings, C in first violins, violas and timpani, followed by the crescendo and uninterrupted finale.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

transitions.title: The basses start running
transitions.from: A · Low strings and horn calls
transitions.to: B · The basses start a fugue
transitions.how: The scherzo closes in C minor. The trio turns to C major and sends cellos and double basses off in running quavers. Successive string entries carry the tune upwards, with bassoons joining the chase. The three-beat bar stays in place.
transitions.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel full score, printed pp. 42–46: C-major trio and successive imitative entries.

transitions.title: The horn call becomes a whisper
transitions.from: B · The basses start a fugue
transitions.to: A′ · Plucked strings and quiet winds
transitions.how: The trio subsides and the low-string arpeggio returns in C minor. Beethoven keeps the scherzo quiet: the repeated-note call passes to clarinets and bassoons, with pizzicato strings around it. The familiar rhythm now comes in small, dry attacks.
transitions.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel full score, printed pp. 45–49: diminishing trio and rescored scherzo return.

transitions.title: Timpani under held strings
transitions.from: A′ · Plucked strings and quiet winds
transitions.how: The detached phrases stop. Cellos and basses hold A♭; first violins and violas hold C, marked pianississimo. The timpani repeat C against that bass. Gradually the violin line moves and the orchestra builds a crescendo, carrying the unsettled chord into the finale’s C major.
transitions.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel full score, printed pp. 50–52. The pedal C is in the timpani; the string bass begins on A♭.

source.title: Beethoven, Symphony No. 5, III, Breitkopf & Härtel full score, plate B.5
source.locator: Printed pp. 37–51: low-string opening, horn calls, C-major fugato, plucked return and timpani bridge into the finale.

timeline.note: Cellos and double basses begin the quiet rising arpeggio in C minor.
Quiet violin phrases answer the low strings, with winds and horns beneath them.
The horns sound their repeated-note call above the strings.
Winds, brass and timpani join the strings in the scherzo’s forceful closing phrases.
Cellos and basses launch the quick C-major fugue subject.
Violas, violins and bassoons join the running subject in successive entries.
Woodwinds punctuate the strings’ overlapping phrases.
The opening low-string arpeggio returns quietly, before the plucked continuation.
Quiet woodwinds trade the repeated notes with plucked and lightly bowed strings.
The timpani repeat C against the A♭ held by cellos and basses.
The violin line rises above held lower strings and the timpani’s repeated C.
Woodwinds, horns and trumpets join the crescendo towards the finale.

composer.epithet: He could make a symphony out of four notes, and spent his last years finding things four string players had never said.
facts: Neefe in Bonn; Haydn, Albrechtsberger and Salieri in Vienna
Bonn until 1792; Vienna and its surrounding villages for the rest of his life
Nine symphonies · five numbered piano concertos · 32 numbered piano sonatas · 16 string quartets · Fidelio
Described his hearing loss in 1801; used conversation books from 1818

quote.text: I live only in my notes.
quote.source: Beethoven to Franz Gerhard Wegeler, Vienna, 29 June 1801; our translation

composer.background:
In March 1778 Johann van Beethoven advertised a concert in Cologne by his six-year-old son. Ludwig was seven. His father, a singer in the electoral chapel at Bonn, hoped to launch another child prodigy; his grandfather, also Ludwig, had risen from singer to Kapellmeister in the same establishment. The boy was baptised on 17 December 1770, probably the day after his birth. Music was the family trade. By his teens he was playing the organ for services and the viola in the court orchestra, learning operas from the middle of the string section.

Christian Gottlob Neefe put Bach’s Well-Tempered Clavier before him and helped him into paid employment. The Breuning household supplied books, friendship and a refuge from Johann’s drinking. After his mother died in 1787, Beethoven increasingly supported his younger brothers. In November 1792 the elector sent him to Vienna to study with Haydn. He was supposed to come back. French troops occupied Bonn in 1794, and the court that paid him disappeared.
